title: Ninety day curriculum
note: Sequenced by domain, following the phasing in the product requirements: financial and council first because the sources are best structured, infrastructure and planning second because the document work is heaviest, community, public safety and synthesis last. Each unit is one primer, one reading assignment, one set of questions, and one written reflection. Coverage is tracked locally in this browser and is not transmitted anywhere. Whether the sequence should instead follow the council calendar so that study tracks upcoming decisions is an open question for the working session.

units.title: What a municipal council actually is
units.primer: An Ontario council acts only by resolution or by-law, at a properly constituted meeting. Individual members, including the head of council, have no authority to direct staff or bind the municipality on their own.

reading.why: The rules the council has adopted for its own conduct: notice, quorum, motions, closed sessions, delegations.

questions: What does the procedural by-law require for an item to reach the agenda?
Who controls the agenda, and by what mechanism?
What must a resolution to close a meeting state?
units.reflection: In three sentences, describe what powers the head of council actually holds and what powers they do not.

units.title: The staff report as an instrument
units.primer: The staff report states the recommendation, the background, the financial implications, and the alternatives. Reading the report rather than the minutes is the difference between knowing what was decided and knowing why.

reading.locator: Three recent staff reports of any kind
reading.why: Learn the house format: where the recommendation sits, where financial implications sit, whether alternatives are genuinely canvassed.

questions: What sections does every report in this township contain?
Where in the report does the cost appear, and is the ongoing operating cost separated from the capital cost?
Are alternatives presented with enough detail to be chosen?
units.reflection: Note one thing the report format makes easy to see and one thing it makes easy to miss.

units.title: The Financial Information Return: what it is
units.primer: Every Ontario municipality files a standardized annual return on the same schedules. It is the only genuinely multi-year, comparable financial source available without transcribing budget books.

reading.locator: Most recent filed year, all schedules, skim only
reading.why: Orientation. Learn what lives in which schedule before trying to extract anything.

questions: Which schedule holds revenue, which holds expenses, which holds reserves?
How long after year end is the return filed?
What does the return not tell you that the audited statements do?
units.reflection: List the three schedules you expect to use most and why.

units.title: Levy, rate, and assessment
units.primer: Council sets a levy, not a tax bill. The levy is divided across the assessment base by class using rates and ratios, so the rate and the levy move independently.

reading.why: See rates and ratios by class, and how they changed.
The assessment base the rates are applied to, and its valuation date.

questions: What is the current assessment valuation date?
Which classes carry which ratios, and when were the ratios last reviewed?
How much of last year's levy increase came from new assessment rather than a rate increase?
units.reflection: Explain to a resident, in plain language, why the rate can rise while their bill stays flat.

units.title: The three portions of the tax bill
units.primer: A North Glengarry bill carries a township portion, a county portion, and an education portion. Council controls the first, votes on the second at a different table, and controls none of the third.

reading.why: The county levy and how it is apportioned among member municipalities.
The township portion, for comparison.

questions: What share of a typical bill is each portion?
How is the county levy apportioned between member municipalities?
How has each portion moved over five years?
units.reflection: Write the single sentence you would use in a debate to describe the tax increase accurately.

units.title: Operating versus capital
units.primer: Operating must balance by law and covers running the place this year. Capital covers building and replacing assets that last decades and is funded from reserves, debt, grants, and a transfer from operating.

reading.why: See how the two budgets are presented and how they connect through the transfer to capital and reserves.

questions: What is the transfer from operating to capital and reserves this year?
What share of the capital budget is renewal and what share is new or expanded?
Which capital projects are grant-dependent?
units.reflection: State the transfer to capital as a percentage of the levy and note whether the budget presents it that way.

units.title: Week one review
units.primer: Consolidate. The first week established how decisions are made and how money is raised and classified.

reading.why: Read a complete package end to end now that the format is familiar.

questions: What could you now answer that you could not a week ago?
Where did the documents not say what you expected?
What is the single largest hole in your understanding?
units.reflection: Write half a page on how the township raises and classifies money, without notes.

units.title: Reading the reserve continuity schedule
units.primer: Reserves are the municipality's savings. Discretionary reserves can be redirected by council; obligatory reserve funds are restricted by statute and cannot be.

reading.why: Opening balance, contributions, withdrawals, closing balance, by reserve.

reading.locator: Note on reserves and reserve funds
reading.why: The purpose-level detail the return flattens.

questions: What share of the total is restricted?
Which reserves have declined and which have grown?
What did the largest withdrawal of the most recent year fund?
units.reflection: Record the discretionary balance separately from the total and note the difference.

units.title: The reserve position over five years
units.primer: A total reserve figure conceals the split between what council can spend and what it cannot. Read reserves by purpose or the picture inverts.

reading.why: Build the series yourself. The act of transcribing it is the point.

questions: Which direction is the discretionary balance moving?
Is there a council-adopted reserve policy with target balances?
How many years of the current renewal shortfall could the discretionary balance absorb?
units.reflection: Enter the five-year reserve series into the dashboard data files and mark it sourced.

units.title: Debt and the Annual Repayment Limit
units.primer: The province caps annual debt repayment at 25 percent of own-source revenue. Distance from the limit describes borrowing room, not whether past borrowing was sound.

reading.locator: Schedule 70 and the Annual Repayment Limit statement
reading.why: Principal outstanding, annual servicing, and the ministry's own calculation of room.

questions: What is the current limit and how much of it is used?
What did the most recent debenture fund, and over what term?
Is the asset it funded still delivering the service it was issued for?
units.reflection: State the borrowing room in dollars of annual servicing, not as a percentage.

units.title: Budget versus actual
units.primer: Variance is actual minus budget. Neither direction is good or bad on its own; the reason is what matters and it is in the year-end report.

reading.why: Actuals by department.
The approved figures to measure against. Note where the groupings differ.

questions: Which departments vary most, and are the same ones varying every year?
Which variances are weather-driven?
Where do the two documents group departments differently?
units.reflection: Build the reconciliation between budget groupings and statement groupings once, and record it.

units.title: Grants and transfers
units.primer: Grants are formula-driven or episodic. Formula allocations can be planned against; project grants arrive when programmes open, which usually determines project timing.

reading.why: OMPF and Canada Community-Building Fund allocations, plus any project-specific agreements.
Total received by year, for the trend.

questions: Which grants are formula-driven and predictable?
What is the trajectory of the unconditional allocation?
Which capital projects proceeded only because a grant was obtained?
units.reflection: List every grant programme the township has drawn on in five years and its cadence.

units.title: Assembling the financial trend
units.primer: Five-year series are the default view in this dashboard. Today you build one properly and see what transcription actually costs in time.

reading.why: Levy, total revenue, and total expenses, transcribed by hand.

questions: Did expenses grow faster or slower than the levy?
What covered the difference?
What price index should this dashboard use to state real changes?
units.reflection: Choose a deflator, record the choice and the reason, and apply it consistently from here.

units.title: Week two review
units.primer: Consolidate the financial position: what is raised, what is owed, what is saved, and what is restricted.

reading.why: What the auditor thought worth drawing attention to.

questions: What is the single most important financial fact you have learned?
Which figure would you most want verified before quoting it publicly?
What is still missing?
units.reflection: Write the township's financial position in one paragraph, descriptive, no adjectives of judgement.

units.title: The strategic plan
units.primer: The plan states council's priorities. Whether they carry measures is a separate question from whether they are the right priorities.

reading.why: Priorities as written, and the measures where they exist.

questions: How many priorities carry an explicit measure?
Which are stated as outcomes and which as activities?
Does council receive a progress report, and on what cycle?
units.reflection: For each priority without a measure, propose one that uses data the township already produces.

units.title: Priorities against the budget
units.primer: Where budget decisions are made independently of stated priorities, the budget is the operative strategy regardless of what the plan says.

reading.why: Whether budget reports reference the strategic priorities at all.
For comparison.

questions: Are budget items presented against priorities?
Which priority received the largest budget allocation?
Which received none?
units.reflection: Record whether the plan is operative in the budget process, with evidence for the answer.

units.title: Building the decision record: method
units.primer: The decision record is the spine connecting every figure in this dashboard to the choice that produced it. Today you establish how to build it.

reading.locator: One year of minutes, index only
reading.why: Identify which decisions are worth recording and which are routine.

questions: What makes a decision worth recording here?
How will you record a decision with no recorded vote?
How will you exclude personal information consistently?
units.reflection: Write the inclusion rule for the decision record and apply it from here without exception.

units.title: Decision record: the current term
units.primer: Transcribe. Volume matters more than commentary at this stage; the analysis comes once the record exists.

reading.why: Date, body, decision, report number, vote, and what it connects to.

questions: Which decisions departed from the staff recommendation?
Which carried a recorded vote, and why those?
Which decisions moved a number elsewhere in this dashboard?
units.reflection: Enter at least ten decisions into the decision record with report numbers.

units.title: Closed sessions
units.primer: Meetings are open by default. Closure is permitted only for enumerated purposes and the resolution must state which.

reading.locator: Closed session resolutions across two years
reading.why: Which exceptions are cited, and how often.

questions: Which exception is cited most often?
What share of meetings included a closed session?
Who is the township's closed meeting investigator?
units.reflection: Record the closed session share by year, descriptively, with no inference about propriety.

units.title: The county table
units.primer: Township council members also sit on county council, which decides county roads, paramedics, social services, and several planning approvals affecting the township.

reading.why: One recent county agenda package, read as a township member would.

questions: Which county decisions in the past year affected North Glengarry directly?
How is the county levy apportioned?
Where do county and township responsibilities meet and blur?
units.reflection: List the county-decided matters a North Glengarry resident would assume are township matters.

units.title: Week three review
units.primer: Consolidate governance: how decisions are made, recorded, and connected to money.

reading.locator: Your own decision record so far
reading.why: Read your work as a stranger would.

questions: Is the record neutral in language?
Is every entry traceable to a report number?
What would a reviewer challenge?
units.reflection: Rewrite any entry that reads as commentary rather than record.

units.title: Major capital projects
units.primer: Track approved budget, spend to date, and status. Reporting dates differ between projects, so record the as-at date on every figure.

reading.why: Current position on each active project.

questions: Which projects are over budget and what explanation was reported?
Which are grant-conditional?
Which are county projects inside the township?
units.reflection: Populate the major capital projects table with as-at dates on every row.

units.title: Water and wastewater as a rate business
units.primer: Water and wastewater are meant to be user-pay and full-cost recovering. Where they are not, the shortfall is covered from the levy by residents who may not be connected.

reading.why: Whether the rate recovers full cost including renewal, and what the rate path assumes.

questions: Does the rate include a renewal component?
How many properties are connected, out of how many in the township?
When was the rate last reviewed?
units.reflection: State whether the systems are full-cost recovering, citing the page that answers it.

units.title: Comparators: choosing them honestly
units.primer: Comparison is context, not judgement. The comparator set has to be defensible before any comparison is shown.

reading.why: Candidate municipalities: lower-tier Eastern Ontario townships of similar population, assessment base, and road kilometres.

questions: Which municipalities are genuinely comparable and on what criteria?
Which comparisons would be unfair and why?
What would make a comparison misleading even when the arithmetic is right?
units.reflection: Propose a comparator set of four to six municipalities with the criteria written down.

units.title: Verification pass
units.primer: Transcription from PDFs introduces errors. Every financial figure gets a second look against the source before it is treated as fact.

reading.locator: Every figure you have entered so far
reading.why: Re-check each against the source. This is the pass the risk register calls for.

questions: How many errors did you find?
Which figures were ambiguous in the source?
Which need a note explaining the basis?
units.reflection: Flip verified figures from sample to sourced in the data files and record the count.

units.title: Upcoming decisions
units.primer: The forward view: where the next commitments will be made and which figures will move as a result.

reading.locator: Outstanding staff directions and reporting dates
reading.why: What council has asked staff to bring back, and when.

questions: What is council committed to deciding in the next six months?
Which decisions have no date attached?
Which have financial consequences not yet in a budget?
units.reflection: Populate the upcoming decisions table, marking items with no council direction as open.

units.title: Phase one gap audit
units.primer: Before moving on, establish what is missing. Naming a hole is more useful than filling it badly.

reading.why: Audit coverage against the requirements list for the financial and council domains.

questions: Which required items have no source at all?
Which sources were requested and not received?
What needs a formal records request?
units.reflection: Write the records request list with a specific document named for each item.

units.title: Phase one review
units.primer: Phase one is complete. It should be genuinely useful on its own, which is the test the phasing was designed around.

reading.why: One more pass over the statements now that everything else is in place.

questions: Can you answer any factual question about township finances in two minutes, with a source?
Which three figures would you stake a public claim on?
Which would you not?
units.reflection: Have someone ask you five financial questions cold. Record which ones you could not answer with a source.

units.title: The asset management plan: structure
units.primer: O. Reg. 588/17 requires this document and sets what it must contain. It is the anchor of the infrastructure domain and should be read before anything else in it.

reading.why: Orientation: inventory, replacement values, condition, levels of service, lifecycle funding.

questions: Which regulatory phase does the current plan satisfy?
When was it adopted and by what resolution?
What is its forecast period?
units.reflection: Map the plan's sections to the requirements in the regulation and note any that are thin.

units.title: Levels of service
units.primer: The plan states proposed levels of service. They are the standard the renewal requirement is sized against, and they may or may not be what council actually adopted.

reading.why: Technical and community levels of service, and how each is measured.

questions: What service levels are stated, and are they current or proposed?
Did council adopt them explicitly?
Where does actual performance appear beside the stated level?
units.reflection: List the service levels that have a matching actual measurement and those that do not.

units.title: The renewal funding gap
units.primer: Required renewal minus planned renewal. The single most important number in the infrastructure domain, and the one most sensitive to assumptions.

reading.why: The requirement and the assumptions behind it.
The planned side of the subtraction, renewal lines only.

questions: Are both sides stated in the same dollar year?
What would closing the gap require as an annual levy increase?
Which asset class carries the largest shortfall?
units.reflection: Compute the gap yourself from both documents and compare with the plan's stated figure.

units.title: Roads: inventory and surface
units.primer: Surface type drives lifecycle cost more than any other road attribute. Gravel, surface treatment, and asphalt have different renewal economics.

reading.why: Kilometres by surface type and owner.
Which roads inside the township are county assets.

questions: How many kilometres does the township own, by surface?
How many county kilometres run through the township?
Which roads would residents assume are township roads and are not?
units.reflection: Draw the ownership split from memory afterwards and check it.

units.title: Road condition and its date
units.primer: A condition rating describes the road on the day it was surveyed. A rating without a date is an unknown, not good news.

reading.why: Condition ratings, methodology, and the assessment date.

questions: When was the last assessment and what method was used?
What share of the network is rated poor or very poor?
How often is the survey repeated?
units.reflection: Record the assessment date beside every condition figure you enter.

units.title: Bridges and culverts
units.primer: Structures with a span of three metres or more require inspection on a two-year cycle under the Ontario Structure Inspection Manual. Ownership follows the road.

reading.why: Inventory, condition, and recommended work with timing.

questions: How many township structures are there, and how many county?
How many have work recommended within five years?
Are any load-restricted?
units.reflection: List every structure with recommended work and whether it is in the capital forecast.

units.title: Week five review
units.primer: Consolidate the asset picture: what is owned, in what condition, and what renewal costs.

reading.why: Per-asset detail behind the class totals.

questions: Is the gap concentrated or distributed?
Which single asset is the largest unfunded item?
What is the oldest condition assessment you are relying on?
units.reflection: Write the infrastructure position in one paragraph, descriptively.

units.title: Drinking water systems
units.primer: Each municipal residential system is licensed, inspected, and rated separately by the province. Systems are reported individually, never township-wide.

reading.why: Inspection ratings and annual compliance reports by system.

questions: What rating did each system receive, and when?
Were there any non-compliances, and what were they?
What is each system's rated capacity and current average day flow?
units.reflection: Record ratings per system and note why a township-wide average would mislead.

units.title: Wastewater performance
units.primer: Effluent quality is measured against the Environmental Compliance Approval limits. Bypass and overflow events are weather-driven and must be read with that context.

reading.why: Annual performance against approval limits, plus bypass reporting.

questions: How does effluent quality compare with the approval limits?
How many bypass events, and in what conditions?
How close is the plant to its rated capacity?
units.reflection: Note whether the plant is constrained by capacity, by approval limits, or by neither.

units.title: Facilities
units.primer: Facilities are where a council decision most often turns on whether to renew or to close. Condition and replacement value are the two figures to have to hand.

reading.why: Age, area, condition, assessment date, replacement value.

questions: Which facilities are rated poor?
What is the total facilities replacement value?
How old are the condition assessments?
units.reflection: For the facility in the worst condition, find every council decision about it in the record.

units.title: Fleet and equipment
units.primer: Operating past replacement age is a deliberate deferral, not a failure. It transfers cost from capital to maintenance.

reading.why: Age, replacement schedule, and which units are past their date.

questions: How many units are past replacement age?
What is the annual maintenance cost on those units?
Is the replacement schedule reserved for?
units.reflection: Connect the fleet replacement schedule to the reserve balances in the financial domain.

units.title: Stormwater and constraints
units.primer: Stormwater is the least documented asset class in most rural townships. Known constraint areas may exist only in engineering memoranda attached to development applications.

reading.why: Regulated areas and any watershed constraints.
Whether the plan covers this class at all.

questions: Does the asset plan cover stormwater?
Which conservation authorities have jurisdiction and over which parts?
Where are the known constraint areas?
units.reflection: Record what is genuinely unknown here rather than estimating it.

units.title: Renewal by asset class
units.primer: A gap distributed evenly and a gap concentrated in one class call for different decisions.

reading.why: Required, planned, and gap for each class.

questions: Which class has the lowest funded share?
Why are water and wastewater closer to funded?
Which class would you address first, and on what basis?
units.reflection: Populate the renewal-by-class table and check the totals against the headline gap.

units.title: Week six review
units.primer: Consolidate. The infrastructure domain is now the heaviest data set in the dashboard.

reading.why: It reads differently once you know what is behind it.

questions: What does the executive summary omit?
Which figures did you have to compute yourself?
What did the plan assume that you would question?
units.reflection: List the three assumptions in the plan that most affect its conclusions.

units.title: Who decides what
units.primer: In a two-tier county, planning authority is divided. Promising an approval the township cannot grant is the most common error in municipal debate.

reading.why: Which plan is operative and what approval authority it establishes.

questions: Is the county official plan the operative document?
Which application types does the county decide?
Is there a delegation by-law, and what does it delegate?
units.reflection: Write the authority split as a table and verify each row against a document.

units.title: The official plan
units.primer: The official plan sets the long-run structure: settlement areas, agricultural protection, where growth is directed.

reading.why: Where growth is permitted and how much the plan assumes.

questions: Where are the settlement area boundaries?
What growth does the plan assume, and over what horizon?
What does it say about agricultural land?
units.reflection: Note any conflict between where the plan directs growth and where servicing capacity exists.

units.title: The zoning by-law
units.primer: Zoning implements the official plan lot by lot and is what an applicant needs an amendment to. An amendment inconsistent with the official plan requires amending the plan first.

reading.why: Residential zones, permitted uses, and what additional units are permitted as of right.

questions: What housing forms are permitted as of right in the settlement areas?
What additional residential units are permitted?
When was the by-law last comprehensively updated?
units.reflection: Check whether the by-law reflects current provincial requirements on additional residential units.

units.title: Applications and timelines
units.primer: The Planning Act sets timelines after which an applicant may appeal on the basis that no decision was made. A missed timeline transfers the decision from council to a tribunal.

reading.why: Type, date received, date decided, recommendation, decision.

questions: What timeline applied to each application, given when it was received?
What is the median processing time by type?
Were any timelines missed?
units.reflection: Build the application register for one year with dates on every row.

units.title: Appeals
units.primer: Appeal history records where decisions were contested and what the tribunal concluded. It is evidence, not a verdict on planning quality.

reading.why: Cases affecting the township and their outcomes.

questions: Who appealed — applicants or objectors?
What did the tribunal conclude?
What did each appeal cost the township?
units.reflection: Summarise each appeal in two sentences: what was contested and what was decided.

units.title: The servicing ceiling
units.primer: What gates growth in a rural township is rarely policy. It is treatment capacity, and it binds before the official plan does.

reading.why: Rated capacity, current flow, committed allocation, and the assumptions.

questions: What per-unit flow rate is assumed, and when was it validated?
How much capacity is allocated to approved but unbuilt units?
In what year does uncommitted capacity run out at the current rate?
units.reflection: Record the assumptions alongside the headroom figure; they matter more than the figure.

units.title: Week seven review
units.primer: Consolidate planning: what can be built, who decides, and what physically constrains it.

reading.why: The current pipeline in one view.

questions: Which active projects are township decisions and which are county?
Which are capacity-constrained?
Which will reach council in the next year?
units.reflection: Populate the active developments table without recording any applicant names.

units.title: The residential pipeline
units.primer: Approved but unbuilt units measure approved supply, not committed construction. Draft approvals lapse if conditions are not cleared.

reading.why: What is approved, registered, built, and what allocation each holds.
What actually got built.

questions: How many approved units remain unbuilt, and for how long?
Does allocation expire?
Why is construction lagging approval?
units.reflection: Reconcile county-held approvals against township-issued permits and record the method.

units.title: Development charges
units.primer: Whether a development charges by-law exists determines who pays for growth-related infrastructure. Its absence is a finding, not a gap.

reading.why: Whether a by-law is in force, and if so what it charges and funds.

questions: Does the township have a by-law?
If not, what funds growth-related infrastructure?
What would a background study cost and how long would it take?
units.reflection: Record the answer plainly either way, with the document that establishes it.

units.title: Economic development
units.primer: Economic development is run at both tiers. Stated objectives are worth recording even where no measure attaches to them.

reading.why: Initiatives, objectives, and any stated measures.
County-level programmes affecting the township.

questions: What initiatives are running and who funds them?
What objective does each state?
How would anyone know whether they worked?
units.reflection: List each initiative with its stated objective and whether it carries a measure.

units.title: Commercial and industrial
units.primer: Non-residential development affects the assessment mix and therefore the distribution of the levy between classes.

reading.why: Floor area and declared value added, by year.
How the assessment mix has moved.

questions: How much non-residential floor area was added in five years?
How has each class's share of assessment moved?
What serviced employment land is available?
units.reflection: Note whether assessment mix shifts have moved burden between classes.

units.title: Verification pass, phase two
units.primer: Same discipline as phase one. Every infrastructure figure gets a second look before it is treated as fact.

reading.why: Re-check against source.

questions: How many errors did you find?
Which figures were stated in a different dollar year than you assumed?
Which need an explanatory note?
units.reflection: Flip verified figures to sourced and record the remaining sample count.

units.title: Phase two gap audit
units.primer: Name what is missing in infrastructure and planning before moving to phase three.

reading.why: Audit coverage against the requirements list.

questions: Which required items have no source?
Which requests are outstanding?
What needs a formal records request?
units.reflection: Extend the records request list with specific documents named.

units.title: Phase two review
units.primer: The heaviest document work is done. Everything after this depends on it.

reading.why: Final pass with the planning context in place.

questions: Can you explain the renewal gap and its causes without notes?
Can you state who owns each road class?
Can you say what gates growth and why?
units.reflection: Explain the infrastructure and planning position to someone unfamiliar, in five minutes, without notes.

units.title: Census geography
units.primer: The census subdivision matches the municipal boundary. Below that level, geographies stop matching anything a council recognises.

reading.why: Which geographies exist and which match the township.

questions: Which geography matches the municipal boundary exactly?
Which does labour force data use?
Where do county and census geographies diverge?
units.reflection: Write the geography label you will attach to every community figure, and use it without exception.

units.title: Population and age structure
units.primer: Age structure moves slowly and predictably and shows up in service demand a decade later. It is the most forecastable thing about the township.

reading.why: Distribution by age band.
The comparison cycles.

questions: How has the median age moved across cycles?
Which age bands grew and which shrank?
What will the 65 to 74 band be next cycle?
units.reflection: Compute the dependency ratio yourself for each cycle and record the method.

units.title: Households and housing stock
units.primer: Tenure and dwelling type describe the housing the township actually has, which constrains what kinds of household can move here.

reading.why: Tenure, dwelling type, household size.

questions: What share of dwellings are single-detached?
What rental stock exists?
How has household size changed?
units.reflection: Note what housing options a household downsizing in place would have locally.

units.title: Building permits as a growth signal
units.primer: Permits are the township's own record and the most timely growth signal available. A permit is a plan, not a building.

reading.why: Counts, dwelling units, and declared value by type.

questions: How many new dwelling units were permitted each year?
How does that compare with the approved pipeline?
What is declared construction value, and what is it not?
units.reflection: Record the caution about declared value everywhere the figure appears.

units.title: Agriculture
units.primer: Agriculture is the dominant land use. Farm counts falling while average area rises is consolidation, not decline, and the two must be read together.

reading.why: Farm counts, area, types, and operator age across cycles.

questions: How have farm counts and total area moved?
Which farm types are growing and which shrinking?
What share of operators are 55 or over?
units.reflection: State what operator age forecasts about land transfer over the next decade.

units.title: Labour force and its limits
units.primer: Employment data is not reliably available at township level. The smallest acceptable geography is larger than the township and must be named.

reading.why: What exists, at what geography, with what error.

questions: What is the smallest geography with acceptable error?
How many residents commute out of the township?
What are the largest employment sectors?
units.reflection: Record commuting figures; they bear on volunteer recruitment and daytime service demand.

units.title: Week nine review
units.primer: Consolidate the community picture and its geography caveats.

reading.why: One pass over the whole profile now that the pieces are familiar.

questions: Which figures are township-specific and which are not?
Where did you have to state a caveat?
What is genuinely unknown?
units.reflection: Check that every community figure in the dashboard carries its geography label.

units.title: Library and recreation
units.primer: These are the township's own numbers and the least standardised data in the dashboard. They are the only record of residents' actual use of what the township provides.

reading.why: The Ontario Public Library Statistics submission is standardized and multi-year.
Registrations and facility usage, where reported.

questions: How has library circulation moved, and what happened in 2020 and 2021?
Which facilities are used most?
What recreation data exists as a series?
units.reflection: Mark the pandemic-affected years as partial rather than comparing them silently.

units.title: County-delivered services
units.primer: Social housing, child care, and long-term care are county responsibilities reported county-wide. Township-level splits may not exist.

reading.why: Waitlists, capacity, and how they are reported.

questions: What is the social housing waitlist and at what geography?
Is a township split obtainable?
What child care capacity exists in the township?
units.reflection: Label every county figure with its geography and never attribute it to the township.

units.title: Fire: the service model
units.primer: A volunteer service responds from home or work. That fact shapes every number in the domain, including response time.

reading.why: The service model and the depth of response council adopted.

questions: What service model does the township operate?
What depth of response does the plan commit to?
When was the community risk assessment last completed?
units.reflection: Note that the plan's commitment, not a national career-service standard, is the fair benchmark.

units.title: Roster and incidents
units.primer: Roster is the leading indicator for the whole service. Roster size and weekday daytime availability are different figures.

reading.why: Roster, entries and exits, incidents by type.

questions: How many joined and how many left each year?
How many respond to a weekday daytime call?
Where is call growth concentrated?
units.reflection: Separate recruitment from retention in the data; they are different problems.

units.title: Response time and its definition
units.primer: The same service produces very different numbers under different measurement definitions. State what is measured, from what event to what event.

reading.why: Whether response time is reported and how it is defined.

questions: From what event is response time measured?
Has the definition changed across years?
Is it reported as an average or a percentile?
units.reflection: Record the measurement definition beside the figure permanently.

units.title: Apparatus and equipment
units.primer: Apparatus replacement is where the township has full control and a long horizon. Funded status connects directly to the reserve balances.

reading.why: Age, service life, replacement cost, and reserve position.

questions: Which units are past service life?
Which have no reserve?
What does insurance grading for protected properties depend on?
units.reflection: Connect each unfunded replacement to a reserve balance or to its absence.

units.title: Week ten review
units.primer: Consolidate fire. It is the service the township owns outright and controls most directly.

reading.why: Provincial context on incident types and fire loss.

questions: What is the trend in roster against incidents?
What would automatic aid change?
What is the largest unfunded apparatus item?
units.reflection: Write the fire service position in one paragraph, descriptively.

units.title: Policing
units.primer: Policing is the largest public safety line and the one council controls least. The bill is driven by a base cost per property and a calls-for-service component, both calculated provincially.

reading.why: The billing statement, the service model, and detachment statistics.

questions: What drives the base cost and what drives the calls component?
How has cost per property moved?
What geography do detachment statistics cover?
units.reflection: State precisely what council can and cannot influence about this cost.

units.title: Emergency management
units.primer: The Emergency Management and Civil Protection Act sets annual requirements. Currency is checkable and binary.

reading.why: The plan, the annual exercise record, and the compliance filing.

questions: When was the plan last reviewed and adopted?
When was the last exercise?
Is the hazard identification and risk assessment current?
units.reflection: Populate the compliance table with dates and mark anything overdue plainly.

units.title: Paramedic services
units.primer: Land ambulance is an upper-tier service with a council-approved response time standard reported county-wide.

reading.why: Calls, response time performance against the standard, and station locations.

questions: What standard has county council approved?
Is it being met county-wide?
Is a township-level split obtainable?
units.reflection: Label these figures as county-wide and resist attributing them to the township.

units.title: Verification pass, phase three
units.primer: Third and final verification discipline. Community and public safety figures get the same second look.

reading.why: Re-check against source.

questions: How many errors?
Which figures carry a geography that is not the township?
Which are still sample?
units.reflection: Flip verified figures to sourced and record the remaining sample count across all domains.

units.title: Week eleven review
units.primer: Consolidate public safety across all four services and three owning tiers.

reading.why: Reread with the full picture in place.

questions: Who delivers each of the four services?
Which costs can council influence?
Where is the clearest trend?
units.reflection: State each service, its owner, and one sourced fact about it, without notes.

units.title: Stewardship: the renewal gap
units.primer: Synthesis. Seven questions, applied to the most important number in the dashboard: what, why, trend, reading, questions, opportunities, risks.

reading.why: The requirement and its assumptions, reread as synthesis rather than extraction.

questions: Which parts of the causal story are sourced and which are inference?
Where is the record silent?
What would change your reading of it?
units.reflection: Complete the stewardship entry, keeping sourced content and interpretation visibly separate.

units.title: Stewardship: the reserve position
units.primer: Apply the same seven questions to reserves, where the headline figure and the usable figure differ.

reading.why: The discretionary and obligatory split.

questions: What did discretionary withdrawals fund?
Is there a reserve policy with targets?
How would you describe the position neutrally?
units.reflection: Write the trend assessment with an explicit confidence level and the reason for it.

units.title: Stewardship: levy and assessment
units.primer: The most politically charged topic in the dashboard, and the one where neutral construction matters most.

reading.why: Rates and ratios, reread with the assessment context.

questions: Can you state the levy trend without implying a judgement?
What would a neutral reader conclude?
What have you assumed that is not in a document?
units.reflection: Have someone read your entry and tell you whether they can infer your position. If they can, rewrite it.

units.title: Stewardship: the servicing ceiling
units.primer: Where a physical constraint, not a policy choice, sets the limit. Assumptions matter more than figures here.

reading.why: The assumptions behind the capacity analysis.

questions: What single assumption most affects the answer?
What is the lead time from decision to commissioning?
What would you ask the operating authority in writing?
units.reflection: Write the risk entries with explicit leading indicators and thresholds.

units.title: Stewardship: the fire roster
units.primer: A topic where the leading indicator is a roster, not a budget line, and where the causal story is largely undocumented.

reading.why: Roster and incidents, reread as synthesis.
The recruitment pool.

questions: Which causal claims can you source and which cannot you?
What would you need to establish causation?
What questions would you ask the chief in good faith?
units.reflection: Mark every unsourced causal claim as an open question rather than an answer.

units.title: Stewardship: age structure
units.primer: The most predictable variable the township plans against, and the one with the longest lag between cause and consequence.

reading.why: Age, dwellings, and mobility read together.

questions: What is knowable to census precision about ten years out?
Where does the demographic profile hit service demand first?
What policy options exist that do not require new servicing?
units.reflection: Write opportunities that are genuinely available to a township, not to a province.

units.title: Stewardship: measurability
units.primer: Whether council's stated priorities can be shown to have been advanced. A finding about documents, not about performance.

reading.why: Priorities and measures, reread against the budget.

questions: Which priorities could be measured with data already collected?
Is the plan operative in the budget process?
What would a one-page annual progress report contain?
units.reflection: Keep this entry descriptive. It is the easiest topic in the dashboard to write as criticism.

units.title: Neutrality review
units.primer: Success criterion five: a neutral reader cannot tell from the dashboard whether the sponsor supports or opposes the current council.

reading.why: Read everything you have written as an opponent would.

questions: Where does language imply judgement?
Where is interpretation presented as record?
Which entries would embarrass you if published?
units.reflection: Rewrite every sentence that fails. Record how many required rewriting.

units.title: Source library audit
units.primer: If the data files disappeared tomorrow, the source library alone should still be worth keeping. Sources are the asset.

reading.why: Every entry: is it linked, stored, requested, or unavailable?

questions: How many sources have no URL and no stored copy?
Which are still outstanding after three months?
Which need a formal records request now?
units.reflection: Bring every source to linked or stored status, or record explicitly why it cannot be.

units.title: Staleness and refresh cadence
units.primer: Every source has a cadence. Defining it is what keeps the dashboard useful after the campaign.

reading.why: When each source is reissued and how long the lag is.

questions: Which sources refresh annually and when?
Which are irregular?
What is the oldest figure currently displayed?
units.reflection: Record a refresh cadence for every source and a calendar of when each becomes available.

units.title: The two-minute test
units.primer: Success criterion one: any factual question about finances, assets, or decisions answered within two minutes, with a source.

reading.why: Use it as a user, not as its author.

questions: Which questions took longer than two minutes?
Where did navigation fail?
Which figures were hard to trace to a source?
units.reflection: Fix the three slowest paths, then retest.

units.title: Twenty indicators without notes
units.primer: Success criterion four: explain the five-year trend and its causes for at least twenty distinct indicators, without notes.

reading.locator: The indicator list across all domains
reading.why: Choose the twenty you will be accountable for.

questions: Which twenty?
Which causes are sourced and which are inference?
Which would you decline to explain because the record is silent?
units.reflection: Say all twenty out loud. Record the ones you could not complete.

units.title: Questions for staff
units.primer: The questions in every stewardship entry are framed to be asked of staff in good faith. Review the whole set for tone.

reading.why: Read them as a department head would.

questions: Which questions read as gotchas?
Which assume an answer?
Which could not be answered by anyone?
units.reflection: Rewrite any question you would not want asked of you in public.

units.title: Coverage audit
units.primer: Success criterion two: recorded coverage across all seven domains. Check what remains untouched.

reading.why: Sample counts, unsourced figures, and stale panels in one view.

questions: How many figures remain sample?
Which domains are thinnest?
What is the highest-value item still missing?
units.reflection: Write the next ninety days' priorities from the gaps, in order.

units.title: Handover to governing
units.primer: The curriculum ends; the instrument continues. What changes is the cadence, not the discipline.

reading.why: The forward view is now the working view.

questions: What refresh cadence will you actually sustain?
Which sources need a standing request?
Who else should have access, and what would they need explained?
units.reflection: Write the operating routine for the dashboard as a governing tool rather than a study one.
